profiles.subject: Theotokos

overview.text: This icon is associated with Saint Nicholas at Pupishevo in Moscow and a January 25 commemoration. The OCA recounts its rediscovery and healing tradition.
overview.reason: Necessary concise source-bound explanation;substantial modern text is not established as freely reproducible. This is an AI-written summary,not the source author’s wording.

blocks.text: The historical image shows Mary with one hand near her head, while Christ rests across her other arm and holds a written scroll. Smaller inscriptions surround the pair. This particular composition is visually distinct from Joy of All Who Sorrow, where the Theotokos commonly stands among people in distress.

blocks.text: The OCA records the icon’s arrival with Cossacks in 1640 and its later placement in a bell tower. In the received story, a sick woman recognizes the dusty image she had seen in a vision and is healed. The article connects the 1760 feast with that event and notes veneration during the 1771 plague. These miracle claims remain attributed to the church’s account.

blocks.text: The source distinguishes the old Pupishevo church, demolished in the 1930s, from the icon’s later location at Saint Nicholas near Kuznetskaya Sloboda. It also lists copies and September 25 and October 9 observances. The history of custody and the type’s wider reproduction are therefore separate: the displayed reproduction is not a claim that every surviving panel is the same physical Moscow object.
